title: Computational physics
tagline: What to compute when the equation will not solve
summary: Integration of the equations of motion, linear algebra, Monte Carlo methods, fields on a grid, many-particle simulation and the numerical signs of chaos.
overview: Most of the equations in the other courses do not have closed-form solutions. Computational physics is the disciplined replacement of those equations by a finite algorithm whose error you can estimate. The subject is not a programming course. The code is short; the question is whether it computes the thing you think it computes.

Ordinary differential equations come first, because Newtonian mechanics is a system of them: Euler’s method, and why its error forces you on to a Runge–Kutta method, with energy as the diagnostic. Linear algebra is the language of small oscillations, of quantum finite differences and of fitting. Monte Carlo integration and the Metropolis algorithm connect to statistical mechanics. Grids turn Poisson’s equation and the wave equation into matrices. A short molecular-dynamics example and a driven pendulum show many degrees of freedom and sensitive dependence in practice.

Every numerical result in this course should be accompanied by a check against a known limit: energy drift, a halving of the step, or a comparison with an exact solution at a special value of the parameters. A plot is not a check.
outcomes: Integrate a second-order equation of motion and estimate the global error of the method used.
Solve a linear system and a linear eigenvalue problem and know which algorithms are stable.
Estimate an integral and an expectation value by Monte Carlo sampling, with an error bar.
Implement a simple Metropolis simulation of an Ising lattice.
Discretise Poisson’s equation and the wave equation on a grid and state the stability condition.
Recognise sensitive dependence in a numerical trajectory and test it by varying the initial data.

history.title: Runge–Kutta
history.detail: Carl Runge published a systematic method for integrating an ordinary differential equation; Martin Kutta generalised it in 1901 to the family of methods that carries both names.

history.title: ENIAC and the Monte Carlo idea
history.detail: Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann proposed estimating integrals by random sampling while working on neutron transport. Metropolis and Ulam published the method in 1949.

history.title: The Metropolis algorithm
history.detail: The paper of Metropolis, Rosenbluth, Rosenbluth, Teller and Teller gave a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann distribution.

history.title: The fast Fourier transform
history.detail: Cooley and Tukey published an algorithm for the discrete Fourier transform in O(n log n) operations. Gauss had used the idea; the paper made it a tool.

history.title: Verlet’s integration
history.detail: Loup Verlet published an integration scheme for molecular dynamics that conserves energy well over long runs and is still the default in the field.

history.title: Lorenz’s equations
history.detail: Edward Lorenz integrated a three-dimensional model of convection and found that trajectories starting close together diverge, the numerical discovery of sensitive dependence.
